name: Carrholt Lakefront Parka
description: A brutally practical heavy parka designed for the Chicago-Milwaukee lakefront corridor, where winter wind off the water cuts like a blade. The Carrholt Lakefront is filled with recycled synthetic down rated to -30°C, wrapped in a matte-finished ripstop shell that sheds sleet and spray without pretension. Available in three colorways: slate gray, rust brown, and a faded olive that seems to have been designed to look worn from day one. The hood is oversized, adjustable with a single-hand cinch cord, and lined with a short pile fleece that actually keeps ears warm. Four exterior pockets, two interior, and a chest pocket with a waterproof zipper. The fit is boxy enough to layer over thick sweaters or light augmentation frames without binding. This is the coat people actually wear in GLMZ winters — not stylish, not augmented, just deeply, honestly warm.
what_it_says: You are a person who has stood at a bus stop in February wind coming off Lake Michigan and decided never again to be cold. Practicality over fashion, comfort over statement.
worn_by: anyone who walks to work in winter
story_hooks: A distinctive rust-brown Carrholt parka was the last thing a missing person was seen wearing — three witnesses placed her at the lakefront transit hub, but the coat turned up in a Tier 1 resale rack with the lining cut out
Carrholt's newest batch shipped with a factory defect: the chest pocket zipper pull is stamped with what appears to be a corponation logo that Carrholt denies any relationship with
The coat's oversized hood has become a low-tech counter-surveillance tool on the Shelf — no tech required, just pull it forward and most facial recognition loses confidence below 60%
related_entities: Arcturus Defense Solutions ChemoShield BX-2 Dermal Toxin Barrier Implant

physical_description.visual_profile: A blocky, utilitarian silhouette that dominates the frame—broad shoulders, generous body, and a length that reaches mid-thigh. The parka reads as pure function: no tailoring, no flourish, just volume. On a person, it creates an impression of mass and solidity, like wearing a portable shelter.
physical_description.fit: Deliberately boxy and relaxed through the torso and sleeves, with enough room to accommodate layered thermals, subcutaneous augmentation rigs, or light exoskeletons without restriction. The cut prioritizes movement and thermal air pockets over body definition.
physical_description.primary_material: Matte-finish ripstop nylon shell (waterproof, wind-resistant) over recycled synthetic down insulation—sourced from post-consumer synth-fiber waste streams common in GLMZ textile recovery.
physical_description.texture: The outer shell has a subtle grid texture from ripstop weave, slightly matte to avoid shine and glare reflection in snow. The interior fleece lining is soft and densely piled, visibly worn at collar and cuffs. Down clusters visible at any small tears, creating an authentically broken-in appearance.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary colorways: slate gray (industrial, neutral), rust brown (warm, oxidized), or faded olive (deliberately pre-weathered, moss-like). All three read as deliberately desaturated—colors chosen to blend into urban industrial landscapes, not stand out.
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty plastic coil zipper down the front (industrial, not precious), with a storm flap and magnetic snap closures for secondary seal. Hood cinches via a single paracord-style pull—one-handed operation even with augmented fingers or numb hands.
distinctive_features: Oversized, adjustable hood lined with fleece—designed to fit over helmet comms or augmented sensor rigs
Four exterior pockets (two hip, two lower) sized for tools, ammo, or survival kit items
Two interior pockets for documents or temperature-sensitive tech
Waterproof-zipped chest pocket—standard for GLMZ workers carrying credentials or currency chips
Reinforced shoulder and elbow areas showing scuff marks and slight wear
Storm flap extends past zipper to prevent wind intrusion
Drawcord at hem can cinch to waist for custom silhouette
Carrholt logo stamped (not embroidered) on chest—minimal, utilitarian branding
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3-4 (working class, functional)—this is the coat of dock workers, construction crews, water treatment technicians, and anyone who works outside in GLMZ winters. Expensive enough to indicate steady employment, cheap enough that losing it doesn't mean financial ruin.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing a Carrholt Lakefront signals honest labor and climate practicality. It's anti-fashion—a rejection of corpo aesthetic and sub-grade improvisation alike. The wearer is someone who works in weather, values durability over status, and trusts equipment more than augmentation to keep them alive.
physical_description.condition_typical: Always slightly worn—salt stains visible around the hem and cuffs, small tears showing synthetic down peeking through, zipper showing minor corrosion from salt spray, hood interior fleece matted from repeated use, overall patina of actual use rather than showroom condition.
